author: pollybot13
body:
Closes #116503

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where iOS users granting Calendar or Reminders access could see the permission flow remain unfinished until relaunch, even though iOS persisted the grant.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both onboarding and Settings now share a retained EventKit permission requester that owns one long-lived `EKEventStore` across the asynchronous system permission sheet and callback. The requester covers calendar add-only/full access and reminders full access without changing permission semantics or copy.

Apple's EventKit contract recommends keeping an event store long-lived. The previous request paths created temporary stores immediately before starting asynchronous authorization.

## User Impact

Calendar and Reminders permission rows can complete and reconcile immediately after the system choice instead of requiring an app restart.

## Evidence

- Reviewed and signed exact head: `44245a7d53a943c5cff6c206abca9d73abdd54d0`.
- Contributor authorship is preserved: the single code commit remains authored by `PollyBot13`; maintainer-only merge-sync commits were removed.
- Exact-head real-behavior evidence gate: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/30675996706
- Exact-head hosted CI: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/30675997689
  - `ios-build`: Swift lint, Debug build, Release build, focused simulator lifecycle tests, and evidence upload passed. The unrelated release-screenshot tail is still running.
  - `macos-swift`: Swift lint, Release build, and the dependency opt-out contract passed. The broad parallel OpenClawKit suite then had one unrelated outbox timing failure among 1,311 tests; that exact test passed locally in isolation (`1/1`, 0.156s).
  - `checks-node-compact-small-9`: one unrelated QA integration test hit its 120-second per-test timeout after 707 passing tests; the exact file passed locally (`2/2`) in 88.70s.
  - `openclaw/ci-gate`: pending the still-running iOS screenshot tail; it will remain non-green until the two unrelated failed jobs are rerun.
- Exact-head local checks:
  - native i18n verification: `entries=5406 changed=false`
  - Swift format: 362 files checked, 0 changes
  - Swift lint: 362 files checked, 0 violations
  - `git diff --check`: clean
  - fresh autoreview: no findings, confidence `0.98`
- Patch-identical immutable runtime proof: the four Swift/test blobs at exact head are byte-identical to the proven code commit `7cefc4705e97175a3a5127ddef9e915e66b405c8`. On a fresh iPhone 17 simulator running iOS 26.5, the real Calendar and Reminders sheets completed, both rows changed green immediately in the same process, seven focused EventKit/permissions tests passed, and the iOS build succeeded.
- Complete runtime evidence bundle: https://github.com/PollyBot13/openclaw/tree/0c768d4a4cbcb20a93ca563aec49e4c11b196cd5/artifacts/pr-116504/current-head
- Redacted terminal proof: https://github.com/PollyBot13/openclaw/blob/0c768d4a4cbcb20a93ca563aec49e4c11b196cd5/artifacts/pr-116504/current-head/terminal-proof.txt
- Physical-device evidence before the fix: OpenClaw `main` at `85466bd89e748aa2ac972bc31bd03bb9eb5b92c2` on an iPhone XR running iOS 18.7.9. After the Reminders grant appeared not to finish, relaunching showed EventKit status `fullAccess`; a read-only EventKit query found a reminder calendar. This confirms iOS persisted the grant while the app flow had not completed.
- Dependency/lifecycle review covered onboarding and Settings entry points, the retained requester, the async continuation bridge, Calendar/Reminders service siblings, status refresh, and macOS/shared call sites. No blocking finding was found. macOS has no EventKit consumer on this path.
- Current-main integration at `af687f920f61d5f252280c0a0b54ca54fbd058ad`: zero touched-file drift; clean merge tree `ec0b990c8c29b14a94e757351b9b8612e6f95318`.
- A second local exact-head focused `xcodebuild test` attempt was stopped after Xcode stalled before compilation at build-description creation. This is recorded as a local Xcode build-service limitation, not as passing proof; hosted Apple builds and the patch-identical focused/runtime evidence above provide the validation.

No layout or copy changed; the screenshots below are runtime permission evidence rather than visual-design proof.

author: kevinmarko
body:
## Summary
- Design-system audit found 6 ad hoc `<select>`s and 2 ad hoc `<textarea>`s across the Pilots PWA (`AIControlCenter.tsx`, `OptionsMatrix.tsx`, `SettingsManager.tsx` x2, `Observability.tsx`, `StrategyHealth.tsx`, `ValidationTrend.tsx`, `DecisionModal.tsx`), each hand-styled with no consistent label/hint/accessibility treatment — unlike the existing `Input` primitive.
- Adds `Select` and `Textarea` to `webapp/src/components/ui.tsx`, matching `Input`'s contract exactly: `label`, `hint`, `invalid`, `id`/auto-`useId`, `aria-describedby` wiring the hint. `Select` takes `options: { value, label }[]` (all 6 real call sites are flat string lists — no disabled options or optgroups needed) and a `hideLabel` escape hatch for the one call site (ValidationTrend's inline metric picker) that has no visible caption today, applying the label via `aria-label` instead so it still gets an accessible name it previously lacked. `Textarea` adds `monospace`/`spellCheck` since the two real call sites genuinely differ (JSON blob vs. free-text note).
- Adds `.select`/`.select-wrap`/`.textarea`/`.textarea-mono` rules to `index.css`, siblings of `.input` sharing its box model, focus ring, invalid/disabled states, and the `--t-input` 16px floor that stops iOS Safari auto-zoom. `.select` also gets a custom chevron affordance (`appearance: none` + a wrapper `::after` arrow, since Chrome won't render `::after` on a native `<select>` directly) replacing each site's inconsistent (or absent) native arrow.
- Migrates all 8 real usages 1:1 — same `onChange`/controlled `value`/`disabled` wiring, same options offered in the same order, `data-testid`s preserved (`log-level-select`, `trend-metric-select`, `validation-trend-metric-select`) via a new `testId` prop. Several sites previously had ad hoc inline-row label layouts (span + select side by side); those now render as `Select`'s consistent block label-above-field layout, matching `Input` everywhere else in the app — a deliberate visual unification, not a functional change.

## What Is Being Fixed

The `aui:container` tag is deprecated in favor of `clay:container`, but JSPs across the repository still use it and nothing rewrote those usages automatically. Every occurrence had to be found and migrated by hand, so the deprecated tag kept reappearing in new code.

## How It Is Being Fixed

The source formatter already owns this class of mechanical upgrade through the catch-all replacement table, so the change adds an entry there rather than introducing a new check. The entry declares `aui:container` as the pattern and `clay:container` as its replacement, scoped to the `jsp` extension so the rewrite only reaches JSPs. Because the pattern matches the tag name rather than a whole element, the single entry rewrites both the opening and the closing tag.

The accompanying fixtures cover the upgrade catch-all check, asserting that the formatter turns `<aui:container></aui:container>` into `<clay:container></clay:container>`.

author: clayshentrup
body:
Dispatch is what every branch in the language is made of — no `if` on type, no match statement, no method table — and it is written twice: an arm search with scoring in the interpreter, a switch with guard chains in the emitter. Nothing compared the two on the cases that *decide* an arm, only on the cases the corpus happens to contain.

Twenty-two cases, deliberately overlapping, because order and specificity are the contract:

- a literal beside a wildcard that would also match, and the value neither claims
- `none` as an arm of its own, and a value that is not `none`
- a narrow record pattern beside a wide one (`(point 0 0)` before `(point 0 _)`)
- a nested pattern against a value that does not nest
- an err arm beside a value arm, from both sides
- arity choosing the group
- a group called through a value rather than by name

## It finds nothing, so it was proved able to speak

A gate that has never been seen fail is a guess. Inverting the arm score in the interpreter — least specific wins instead of most — makes **eleven of the twenty-two** disagree, each naming the arm the two engines took:

```
  a literal beats a later wildcard
    native: out='zero\n'
    interp: out='any\n'
  none is an arm of its own
    native: out='nothing\n'
    interp: out='something\n'
```

## Two probes read as agreement without being any

`which -0` parses as subtraction, so it tested arithmetic and both engines agreed on the resulting error. And a probe that fails to compile prints the same nothing on both engines — which is how https://github.com/kanso-lang/kanso/pull/530's sweep first read `0 disagree` with every probe broken.

The harness now fails on a probe that did not run or printed nothing at all. Every probe here names the arm that answered, so an empty answer is a broken probe rather than a quiet engine.

28 test binaries green.

body:
## Summary

First slice (**188c1**) of #188. Stands up OpenHuman's real `tinycortex` memory engine **in-process**, replacing the inert `HttpCortexClient` with an engine-backed `CortexClient` (`EngineCortex`) that persists per-company memory on local disk. Ships in **degraded (lexical/recency) recall** mode — zero embedding compute injected — so it works today with no backend service; real vector recall (embeddings + hybrid retrieval + the job queue) is the follow-up slice **188c2** (#201).

The engine crate is already an unconditional dependency of `openhuman_core`; this only *constructs* it. Bridge, not rip-out — `CortexMemoryStore` / `CortexContextStore` / `OcMemory` light up unchanged through the existing `OPENCOMPANY_MEMORY=tinycortex` overlay. No `builder.rs` / `harness` / `ports` changes; the only "hot" edit is an additive branch in `store/select.rs`.

Rebased green on current `main` (the `examples/CompanyRecord` blocker, #194, has merged). Maintainer review (@senamakel) addressed below.

## API Or Behavior Changes

- New `EngineCortex` (`src/store/tinycortex_engine.rs`): per-company workspace at `<data_dir>/memory/<company>/`, `MemoryConfig` built directly with `embedding.strict = false`; all 11 `CortexClient` verbs implemented. In degraded mode chunks/traces/tasks persist via the engine's KV tier and `search_chunks` ranks by lexical token-overlap (the crate's hybrid/graph scorers are wired in 188c2/#201).
- `store/select.rs`: `open_tinycortex` returns `EngineCortex` when a data dir is present, else the in-memory fallback.
- **Loud degraded-mode contract (was a quiet warn — @senamakel point 5):** the surviving engine path now emits a one-time `warn!` naming it *"DEGRADED lexical fallback — substring/recency, NOT vector/semantic recall; real embedding-backed recall lands in #201"* (also in the fn doc + `storage.md`).
- **`tinycortex` memory + `mongodb` storage now REFUSES TO OPEN (was a warn).** That combination makes the pod `/data` ephemeral scratch, so in-pod memory would be silently lost on restart. Rather than warn-and-continue into silent data loss, `open_tinycortex` returns a hard config error naming the fix (mount a persistent volume at `OPENCOMPANY_DATA_DIR`, use `fs`/`sqlite` storage, or keep memory on the base store). `fs`/`sqlite` (durable `/data`) paths unchanged.
- **⚠️ Breaking crate-surface change (@senamakel point 3):** the inert `HttpCortexClient` is **removed** from `src/store` and its re-exports (the managed-REST-service framing is dropped — the engine embeds in-pod). It is genuinely deleted, not renamed; downstreams importing it must migrate to `EngineCortex`/the `CortexClient` trait.
- **Opt-in and additive**: with `OPENCOMPANY_MEMORY` unset the default storage path is byte-identical to today.

## Tests

- [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- [x] `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` (default) — clean.
- [x] `cargo build --all-targets` (default) — passes.
- [x] `cargo test` (default) — **867 + 6 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored**.
- [x] **Full-feature** (@senamakel point 2 — every line here is behind `tinycortex`/`openhuman`, which default CI never compiles): `cargo build --features openhuman,tinycortex --all-targets` passes · `cargo test --features openhuman,tinycortex --lib store::` → **68 passed, 0 failed** (EngineCortex conformance, persistence-across-reopen, two-company isolation, overlay selection, degraded lexical search, **refuse-to-open on ephemeral mongodb**, durable-base-opens) · `cargo check --all-features` passes.
- Full-feature `clippy -D warnings` trips only on **pre-existing vendored** lints (`tinyagents` `large_enum_variant`, `openhuman` unused/dead-code) whose submodule pins are byte-identical to `main`; **zero findings point into this diff**.

The structural gap that made the green default `Rust` check meaningless for a fully-feature-gated diff is filed as **#202** (build/test the `openhuman,tinycortex` sets in CI).

## Documentation

`docs/spec/runtime/storage.md` updated: the in-pod engine, the loud degraded-recall contract, and the durability section now documents **refuse-to-open** (not warn) for `mongodb` + `tinycortex`, referencing #201.

## Related

Part of #188. Follow-up: **#201** (188c2 — real vector recall, stacked on this). CI-gap: **#202**. Depended-on fix (merged): #194.

body:
Five things on the audit-level control page (FY26 ICFR — Altura Infra Group), each raised while walking the screen.

### Extracted by was asked for, not filled in
The person signed in is the person who just ran the extract, so it is stamped in when the population is created, with a line under the field saying where it came from. Still editable — IT often pulls the file — and the other two facts stay asked for, because nothing here can know them.

### The date fields were the operating system's
Three of them — **Extracted on**, and the filter's **Date from / Date to** — now use the shared `DatePicker` already on Home and the Internal Audit tabs: brand selection, month/year drill-down, and `Jul 28, 2026` the way dates read everywhere else. Their wrappers went from `<label>` to `<div>` with an `aria-label`, because a label forwards its clicks into the picker's button and toggles it twice.

### The extract disagreed with the expectation by construction
The count came off the file size, so whatever figure you typed above it, the check opened on a variance — 100 expected against 1,418 extracted, 1318% over. It now lands on the figure written down, a row or two either side, with the wobble sized against the 2% shortfall band so the check reads as a pass; small populations hit exactly. `UNDER_BAND` is exported for it, so the extract measures itself against the same constant the check does and the two cannot drift.

### Manage deficiencies didn't move the tab
Inside an audit, Deficiency management **is** a tab — swapping only the content left the bar reading "Dashboard" over a different page. It sets the tab now, and so do the two year-end checklist rows. Engagement level has no such tab, so there it stays a drill-in.

### The deficiency was graded somewhere else
A control that concludes ineffective raises a finding, and grading it meant leaving the paper for another tab, finding the row, and coming back to a page scrolled elsewhere. The banner is now the toggle and the card opens underneath it — the same card the tab renders, pulled out of `DeficienciesView` as `DeficiencyCard` so severity rules, four-eyes guards and the close/reopen confirms are one implementation rather than two. Collapsed in a list, open on the paper. The modals portal to the body, since this card now lives under animated ancestors that would otherwise capture a fixed backdrop.

## Verification
- `npm run build` (tsc -b && vite build) passes
- Driven in a real browser: the tab moves with the link, the deficiency card opens and shuts in place with the control page staying put, and the Deficiency management list renders unchanged after the extraction

## Note on the base
This branch was behind main; all of `origin/main` through PR #120 is merged in here (that merge was conflict-free), then the work sits on top.

`l1-04-single-servo`. One new file:
`scripts/authoring/l1-04-single-servo/EXAM.json`, seeded by the committed
`scripts/seed-exam.ts`.

### Why this one was rewritten rather than drafted

L1.04's cards were authored to 462 blocks while this bank was being written.
A draft of this exam existed from before that work and it was stale: it
predated six of the eight cards, and one of its layout questions asserted that
the servo rail's ground return needs sizing, which the finished LAYOUT card
explicitly contradicts (the return is a plane, "never the constraint"). So this
bank was rebuilt from a fresh read of all eight cards.

Half the questions test material that exists only in the freshly authored
cards:

- the third net class, and why widening Power instead would fight the routing
  everywhere for a current that never arrives near the USB connector
- a 3 mm section of servo rail at 0.25 mm that passes DRC and still runs hot,
  because the thermal number is only true at the narrowest point
- C8 rated 16 V because D3 clamps at 10.3 V, not because the rail reaches 5.5 V
- the `SS34` suffix that decides the package, where the SMA variant is a
  different part number that will not fit the pads
- `J5` pin 2 labelled `+5V`, which the card calls the one keystroke that
  silently undoes the whole board

Coverage: Requirements 3, BOM sourcing 2, Schematic 3, Layout 3,
DRC + Gerber 1, Ordering 2, Assembly 2, Bring-up 2.

### Distractors

A series diode confused with a shunt crowbar. A flipped crowbar read as
harmless because a two-pin symbol looks symmetric. A bulk capacitor credited
with carrying a sustained stall it explicitly cannot. A cathode band dismissed
as a manufacturing mark.

### Answer key

6 / 6 / 6, counted before seeding.

### Stems

Thirteen scenario, five definition, ending on the lesson's graded moment: a
pinched horn and a serial heartbeat that never skips a line.

### Verification

Seeded against the LOCAL database with the committed seeder: 18 questions,
8 sections, `pos 0: 6 / pos 1: 6 / pos 2: 6`. Zero em-dashes and en-dashes.
`accessTier` and `publishedRevisionId` unchanged.

### Merging this ships nothing

The bank lands on main; the content goes live only when the seeder is run
against prod.

Reviewers: the diff is the exam, answer key included. Read each `correctIndex`.

author: michaelrobertsutton
body:
## Summary

- Bumps `react-router-dom` 6.30.4 → 7.18.2 and adds/updates npm `overrides` for `brace-expansion`, `svgo`, `shell-quote`, `fast-uri`, `http-proxy-middleware`, `body-parser`, `@babel/core`, and `postcss`.
- Closes 13 of the 16 currently-open Dependabot alerts in code. The remaining 3 (`webpack-dev-server`, alerts 35/44/45) have no compatible patch under `react-scripts` 5.0.1 and will be dismissed as `not_used` separately (build-time-only, prod serves a static build via `serve`).
- Adds `frontend/src/setupTests.js` (TextEncoder/TextDecoder polyfill) and a `jest.moduleNameMapper` entry for react-router's `./dom` subpath export — both required for CRA 5's frozen Jest 27 to resolve react-router v7's package structure. Confirmed by reproducing the failure and fixing it, not assumed.

## Alert → fix mapping

| Alert | Package | Installed before | Installed after | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 54 | brace-expansion | 1.1.14 | 1.1.18 | ✅ fixed |
| 53 | body-parser | 1.20.5 | 1.20.6 | ✅ fixed |
| 52, 51 | react-router | 6.30.4 | 7.18.2 | ✅ fixed |
| 50 | react-router-dom | 6.30.4 | 7.18.2 | ✅ fixed |
| 49 | svgo | 1.3.2 / 2.8.2 | 2.8.3 | ✅ fixed (verified with a real SVG-import build probe — see below) |
| 48 | shell-quote | 1.8.4 | 1.10.0 | ✅ fixed |
| 47, 46 | fast-uri | 3.1.2 | 3.1.4 | ✅ fixed |
| 41 | http-proxy-middleware | 2.0.9 | 2.0.10 | ✅ fixed |
| 40 | @babel/core | 7.29.0 | 7.29.7 | ✅ fixed |
| 35, 44, 45 | webpack-dev-server | 4.15.2 | unchanged | dismissal (no compatible patch; see Phase 6 note below) |

Each row above was checked against the actual installed version in `package-lock.json`, not inferred from `npm audit`'s summary.

## A note on `npm audit`'s 53-vulnerability count

`npm audit` reports 53 high-severity findings on this branch. This is a verified **reporting artifact**, not a regression:

- Two brand-new `brace-expansion` advisories were published this week (GHSA-3jxr-9vmj-r5cp on 2026-07-20, GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg on 2026-07-24) extending coverage up to `<=5.0.7`. Neither is among the 16 target alerts.
- Once `brace-expansion` is pinned via an override, `npm audit` can no longer propose a simple version bump as the fix, so it falls back to listing every ancestor in the `eslint`/`jest`/`workbox` dependency chains (all build-time-only, never shipped) instead of one line item.
- The correct fix for alert 54 uses a version-qualified override key (`"brace-expansion@1": "^1.1.16"`) so only the 1.x instance (used by `minimatch@3.1.5`, itself only used by eslint/jest/workbox at build time) is touched — the `filelist` package's `minimatch@5.1.9` still gets its own compatible `brace-expansion@2.x`. Verified via `npm ls brace-expansion`.
- Escaping the newer, broader advisory (`<=5.0.7`) would require forcing `brace-expansion@5.x` onto `minimatch@3.1.5`, a package frozen inside `react-scripts` since 2022 — real compatibility risk, not required by any of the 16 target alerts, and out of scope here.

## New advisory found during this work (not yet a Dependabot alert on this repo)

`npm audit` also flags `react-router-dom@7.18.2` against GHSA-qwww-vcr4-c8h2 ("RSC Mode CSRF Bypass"), published 2026-07-24 — 6 days before this branch. Read the advisory text directly: **it only affects apps using the unstable RSC APIs.** Lenny uses none (`BrowserRouter`/`Routes`/`Route`/`Link`/`NavLink`/`Navigate`, no RSC). Staying at 7.18.2 is correct; escaping this advisory would require react-router v8 (a major bump — alerts 51/52 require ≥7.18.0, so every 7.x that closes them sits inside this advisory's range; 8.0+ is the only version outside it). GitHub's own Dependabot scan hasn't picked this up yet — it plausibly will shortly after this merges. Flagging now so a future alert here isn't a surprise.

## Verification

- Lint: `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` — clean (unchanged from main, no backend code touched).
- Unit: 503 passed, 0 failed.
- CI-equivalent integration suite (real HAPI containers): 29 passed, 7 skipped, 0 failed.
- `npm run build`: compiles successfully, including the SVG-import svgo probe (temporarily wired a real SVG import through `@svgr/plugin-svgo` — the one path the flat `svgo` override could have silently broken — confirmed clean, then removed the scratch files).
- `npm test -- --watchAll=false`: all 6 suites, 88/88 tests pass (required the two jest fixes above; failed without them — this is the one thing CI itself never runs, so it needed this level of scrutiny).
- `npm start`: dev server compiles and serves (confirms `webpack-dev-server` 4.x + `shell-quote`/`http-proxy-middleware`/`body-parser` overrides didn't break the dev server).
- Full local docker stack, walked with a real browser:
  - `/` → redirects to `/measures`; `/measures`, `/jobs`, `/results`, `/validation`, `/settings` all load with zero console errors.
  - Clicked the `Calculate` link on a measure row — confirmed the `Link to={/jobs?newCalc=...}` query-param navigation from `MeasuresPage.js` works correctly with react-router v7.
  - Ran a full measure calculation through the UI (CMS122, 56 patients) end to end, then navigated into `/results/1` (`useParams` route) and confirmed patient-level results render correctly.
  - Uploaded a validation bundle and ran a full validation through the UI (CMS124, 33 patients, 100% pass rate) with zero console errors.
- `npm audit`: 13/16 target alerts confirmed closed by direct version check (see table above); the artifact-count caveat is documented above rather than glossed over.

## Pre-existing bug found during this work (out of scope, filed separately)

While walking every route, `/groups` returned a raw server 404 on direct navigation. Root cause: `frontend/public/serve.json`'s `rewrites` list has an entry for every other client route (`/measures`, `/jobs`, `/results`, `/results/:jobId`, `/validation`, `/settings`) but is missing `/groups` — unrelated to this PR, predates it, and would behave identically on react-router v6. No nav link currently exposes `/groups`, so blast radius is low. Filed as a separate issue rather than fixed here to keep this PR scoped to the security patch.

## Related issue

N/A — see the separate issue filed for the `/groups` finding above.

## Type of change

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Refactor / cleanup
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Infrastructure / CI/CD
- [x] Chore (deps, tooling, lockfile)

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added or updated (setupTests.js polyfill + jest config, required for react-router v7 under CRA's Jest)
- [ ] docs/ updated (if architecture or API changed) — N/A, no architecture change
- [x] No new ADRs needed, OR I've added an entry to `docs/decisions.md`
- [x] Security implications considered — this PR's entire purpose is closing security alerts; see mapping table and audit-artifact/new-advisory notes above

## Test plan

- `cd frontend && npm ci && npm run build && npm test -- --watchAll=false`
- `cd backend && ruff check app/ tests/ && python3 -m pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/integration`
- `./scripts/run-integration-tests.sh --ignore=tests/integration/test_golden_measures.py --ignore=tests/integration/test_connectathon_measures.py --ignore=tests/integration/test_full_workflow.py --ignore=tests/integration/test_groups_dropdown.py --ignore=tests/integration/test_full_jobs_pipeline.py --ignore=tests/integration/test_factory_reset.py`
- `docker compose up -d --build`, then walk `/measures` → click Calculate → run a measure calc → view `/results/:jobId`, and `/validation` → upload a bundle → run a validation.

author: robinsongalvis
body:
Tercer PR de la Fase 1, y el peor nudo. Sombras 29 → 4. Deriva total 89 → 64.

  --sombra-1: 0 5px 15px         apoyado en la página
  --sombra-2: 0 10px 30px        levantado: hover, paneles
  --sombra-flotante: 0 12px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.3)   despegado del papel
  --brillo: 0 0 20px rgba(212,175,55,0.35)         encendido, no elevado

Dos de los 29 valores no eran sombras, y por eso no bajaban:

  El ANILLO. Un "0 0 0 2px" no tiene ni desplazamiento ni desenfoque: es un
  borde dibujado con box-shadow para no ocupar espacio. No dice altura. Se
  reconoce por su forma, no por una lista de excepciones.

  El BRILLO. Tampoco dice altura: dice que algo está encendido. Es la vela
  prendida, el tema elegido, el momento bajo el dedo. Merece su propio token.

LOS DOS PRIMEROS TOKENS LLEVAN SOLO LA GEOMETRÍA, y el color se pone al usarlos. Esto empezó como una regresión que introduje yo: puse el color adentro del token, y un var() dentro de la declaración de otra variable se resuelve donde se DECLARA, no donde se usa. Quedó congelado con el color del tema por defecto y los ocho estados de tema perdieron el tinte de su sombra —en fondo oscuro, una sombra invisible—. Verificado tras el arreglo: los ocho lo conservan, del naranja de atardecer al azul de noche.

El hover de la tarjeta del timeline recupera su elevación: antes subía Y brillaba, y al tokenizar se quedó solo con el brillo. Ahora es "var(--sombra-2), var(--brillo)": la sombra dice la altura, el brillo dice el foco. Y el ícono deja de tener una sombra propia en hover, porque el volteo de fondo a dorado ya es la respuesta.

Se tapó un hueco que dejé en el PR de los radios: siete radios vivían en border-top-left-radius y compañía, y el guardián solo miraba la propiedad corta. Ahora mira las cinco formas.

El guardián cambió en tres cosas:
  · Cuenta sombras sueltas, no declaraciones. Antes, combinar dos valores del
    sistema —"var(--sombra-2), var(--anillo)"— contaba como inventar un tercero.
  · Ignora los anillos por su forma: ^0 0 0 \d.
  · QUITA LOS COMENTARIOS antes de medir. Sin eso, un comentario que explique
    una regla se mide como si fuera la regla. Pasó documentando este archivo:
    el guardián reportó 9 sombras, y cuatro eran prosa mía.

Verificado por ataque: bloquea una sombra literal nueva, un brillo distinto y un radio en formato largo. NO bloquea cambiar el grosor de un anillo, y es deliberado: un anillo es un borde, y el guardián no audita bordes. Queda como límite conocido, no como cobertura.

Nota honesta sobre el método: este panel de pruebas congela las transiciones, y .message-card tiene transition sobre box-shadow. Durante un rato el navegador me devolvió el valor viejo y casi reporto una regresión que no existía. Se confirmó desactivando la transición y volviendo a medir.

Queda anotado para la Fase 2: en modo oscuro --border-soft es rgba(255,255,255,0.05), o sea BLANCO. Las tarjetas no tienen sombra, tienen un halo: se ven como si emitieran luz. Se conservó tal cual porque el color es decisión de la fase de identidad, no de ésta.

## New islands

author: coreyloftus
body:
## Summary

Recording was blocked by a Screen Recording prompt that reappeared on every attempt, while System Settings still listed the app as allowed. Re-toggling it there did nothing. Two independent causes, both in how the bundle was signed and described.

- **Ad-hoc signing pinned the TCC grant to the binary's cdhash.** With no Team ID and no designated requirement, macOS falls back to `designated => cdhash H"..."`, so any rebuild — or an OS update, which is what actually triggered this (macOS 27 Beta 2 on Jul 25) — silently voids the grant. The Settings row is keyed on bundle path, so it keeps displaying the app as approved while `tccd` refuses to match it.
- **`scripts/setup_signing.sh` (new)** creates a stable self-signed identity in a dedicated keychain, so signing never needs the login-keychain password. Both build scripts now use it and warn loudly if they fall back to ad-hoc. The resulting requirement, `identifier "com.meetingscribe.app" and certificate leaf = H"..."`, survives rebuilds.
- **`Info.plist` was missing `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`.** ffmpeg captures the mic as a child of `scribed`, which the app spawns, so TCC attributes the request to this bundle — and with no usage string macOS *kills* the requesting process instead of prompting. Microphone has no "+" button in System Settings, so it couldn't be granted by hand either. Latent for months behind an older grant; only surfaced once that grant was reset.
- **Screen Recording preflight** in `AppState.startRecording()`, so the prompt is raised deliberately instead of surfacing as a bare system dialog mid-record with a 500 blaming "the terminal".
- **`specs/bundle-distributable-app.md`** — spec for turning the app into a distributable DMG, written for autonomous execution by a fresh agent.

## Test plan

- [x] `setup_signing.sh` creates the identity; re-running is idempotent
- [x] Designated requirement is cert-anchored, not cdhash (`codesign -d -r-`)
- [x] Re-signing twice leaves the requirement byte-identical — the property that fixes the bug
- [x] `codesign --verify --strict` passes on the signed bundle
- [x] `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` present in the installed bundle
- [x] `build_helper.sh` runs end-to-end: compiles and signs `bin/syscap`
- [x] Recording works end-to-end — `POST /v1/start` returns 200, both WAVs grow
- [x] Captured audio is real signal, not silence: system `mean_volume -23.4 dB`, mic `-36.0 dB`
- [ ] **`build_app.sh`'s new signing block never executed** — its `swiftc` step fails on this toolchain, so signing was applied by running the equivalent `codesign` invocation by hand. The script path itself is unverified.
- [ ] **`AppState.swift` preflight never compiled** — parses clean under `swiftc -parse` only
- [ ] Rebuild-survival test (rebuild, then record without re-prompting) — blocked on the same toolchain issue

## Notes

**The SwiftUI app cannot currently be built.** Command Line Tools 27.0 beta 4 (installed Jul 27) made `@State` a macro, and bare CLT ships no `SwiftUIMacros` plugin — ~48 errors, with misleading `cannot find '$x' in scope` cascades downstream. Needs full Xcode or a CLT downgrade. This is pre-existing and unrelated to these changes.

Everything shipped here was therefore applied by patching and re-signing the existing binary, which needs no toolchain. The two unchecked Swift-dependent boxes above should be closed on the first successful build.

The signing identity's private key lives in the `meeting-scribe-signing` keychain, with a backup at `~/.config/meeting-scribe/signing/` (outside the repo, so it can't be committed). If both are lost the cert changes and TCC breaks again — `setup_signing.sh` regenerates a *new* identity, it does not recover the old one.

author: 0xsoftboi
body:
Started as "add bridge providers." Ended up fixing **three pre-existing production bugs**, giving bridging a UI it never had, and finding four more bugs by actually deploying and running it. Review the production bugs first — they matter more than the feature.

**Verified in dev**: deployed to `python-api` (dev), USDT0 enabled, live API returns real 1:1 routes on every corridor, 8/8 attempts, no RPC pinning.

---

# ⚠️ Pre-existing production bugs fixed here

### 1. The generic CCTP rail burned USDC that was never minted

`swap_engine.py:862`/`:2334` offered CCTP on the **live** quote path; `:2739` dispatched it; `_execute_cctp_swap` did approve → burn → `return` and **stopped**. Nothing polled the attestation or called `receiveMessage`. `cctp_relayer.py` only serves HyperCore and is funded for HyperEVM gas, so it could not complete a generic burn, and `cctp_api.build_receive_transaction` had **zero callers**.

Funds destroyed, not delayed. Gated off immediately, then a real completion relayer built so the rail can be turned back on.

### 2. `encode_abi(fn_name=...)` crashes on the pinned web3

`requirements.txt:401` pins `web3==7.16.0`, which renamed that parameter. Reachable via `POST /webapp/swap/build` → ERC20 approve (`swap_engine.py:1166`), so **first-time token approvals were crashing for external-wallet users**. 9 sites fixed, plus a guard test that also asserts the kwarg still raises so it cannot rot into a no-op.

### 3. Provider dispatch failed open to Li.Fi

`execute_swap`'s chain ended in `else: _execute_lifi_swap`, so any unrecognised provider was executed by the **Li.Fi executor against a foreign quote**. `provider` is caller-supplied on the internal/webapp paths (`qd.get("provider", "lifi")`), and the bridge registry can surface providers with no executor. Now an allowlist checked before locks or fund movement, with a drift test that parses the dispatch chain so it cannot diverge.

---

# Bugs found by deploying (none of which mocks could catch)

- **`quoteSend` blocked the event loop.** `web3.py`'s `.call()` is synchronous and was invoked inline in `async def get_quote`. Fine against fast Arbitrum; against Ethereum it stalled the API until health checks failed and Railway restarted the service. Mocked tests structurally cannot catch this — the mock returns instantly.
- **RPC health checks only probed `eth_blockNumber`.** An endpoint serving that but rejecting `eth_call` passed as healthy and broke **every contract read**, surfacing as an innocuous empty route list. The culprit was **`meowrpc.com`** (Ethereum, Base and Arbitrum all answer *"The method eth_call is not supported"*).
- **Cold-start endpoint roulette.** The first sweep waited 30s and chainlist endpoints were appended after it, so they were never probed before becoming selectable; unprobed endpoints score like proven ones, making selection a coin flip right after deploy. Now probed at startup and at discovery, with a genuine method-not-found quarantined on first sight.
- **My own fix was too broad**, and dev caught it in a minute: treating *any* `eth_call` error as unsupported permanently evicted Flow's node, which had **executed** the probe and rejected the synthetic payload. Only `-32601`/explicit "not supported" counts now.

Also fixed: **Plasma had no RPC endpoint from any source**, making the `arbitrum↔plasma` USDT0 corridor unquotable — the corridor USDT0 exists for on Plasma, which has no native USDT. And `eth.llamarpc.com` (HTTP 403) removed from both the defaults and the trusted domains.

---

# Feature work

**Bridge abstraction** (`bot/services/bridge/`) — ~15 providers were duck-typed into `SmartRouter` with no shared interface. Adds a `BridgeProvider` ABC + `BridgeQuote` modelling **settlement** (`tx`/`deposit_address`/`canonical`) and **trust model** (`liquidity`/`canonical`/`solver`) as first-class fields. Providers: NEAR Intents, Allbridge Core, Symbiosis, Arbitrum canonical (deposit only — withdrawal refused, since a ~7-day challenge period would be misleading as a swap quote), USDT0.

**Not built directly:** Synapse, Celer, Hop, Stargate — already routed via Li.Fi/Socket, and Stargate's legacy API is mid-deprecation toward LayerZero's Value Transfer API.

**CCTP v1 → v2** — v1 is deprecated by Circle. Fast Transfer settles ~8-20s vs ~13min. Defaults to **Standard** so nobody silently starts paying Fast fees; `maxFee` bounded with integer math that refuses rather than submitting unbounded.

**Stable-aware routing** — `is_usdc` was computed at `router.py:127` and used in exactly one place, never reaching scoring, so CCTP was ranked identically to pooled bridges despite being zero-slippage. Stable pairs now prefer native 1:1 rails, with non-stable scoring pinned byte-identical by a regression test.

**Bridge UI** (`/bridge` in the terminal) — bridging previously had no surface at all outside `/btc`. Organised around the idea that a bridge is a **custody hand-off**: the `CustodyTimeline` draws the transit gap as a real span with the trust model named inside it, routes are ranked on what arrives **net of cost** (never headline output), and in-flight state says plainly that funds have left one chain and not arrived at the other.

**Signing + status** — `POST /bridge/build` issues the `transferId` and writes the row **before** anything is signed, because a signed bridge tx with no row is invisible forever. `/bridge/record` is idempotent; `/bridge/transfers/{id}` derives CCTP state from the relayer rather than keeping a second copy that can disagree.

**On-chain verification** — `scripts/verify_onchain_constants.py` checks every CCTP address and domain, `usedNonces`, all USDT0 token/OFT pairs via `OFT.token()`, decimals, the per-chain `approvalRequired()` asymmetry, and all 8 LayerZero EIDs against live chains. Non-zero exit on mismatch. Unit tests cannot catch a wrong address — they assert against the same constant.

---

# Review history

Three Opus money-path reviews: **BLOCK** (13), **SHIP WITH FIXES** (6), **BLOCK** (2 critical + 8). All fixed, fail-closed. Including two where my own reasoning was wrong:

- **Idempotency by revert-string.** The relayer decided "already minted" by matching revert text, applied to broadcast errors dominated by *EOA* nonce collisions that some RPCs word identically — marking deposits minted that never minted, invisible to both retry paths. Replaced with `MessageTransmitterV2.usedNonces`, verified live.
- **My pooled-bridge discount was wrong.** I penalised non-native providers on stable pairs for "unpriced spread", but Across quotes a guaranteed fill and CoW settles at a signed limit price, while CCTP-Fast was the rail with the genuinely unpriced fee. ~$200 worse on a $10k bridge. Removed.
- **My fee ceiling was wrong.** A fixed `0.05` *native units* is ~$150 in ETH but ~a cent in XPL, so it passed on Ethereum and rejected **every** legitimate Plasma quote. Now USD-denominated.

---

# CI

Red for **two pre-existing reasons, both present on `main`**: the same 2 `test_webapp_limit_orders` failures (full-suite order pollution — they pass in isolation, on pristine HEAD, and with this branch's test files removed) and a showcase stats-drift check in a directory this branch never touches.

`main`: 1179 passed, 2 failed. This branch: **1363 passed, 2 failed.** 184 more passing tests, zero new failures.

# ⚠️ Before enabling anything in production

Every provider is **default-OFF**. See `docs/deployment/bridge-rails-runbook.md`.

**The signed transfer has never happened.** The executor path — approve, chain switch, send, record — has not run against a real wallet, because the flow is non-custodial and needs a wallet holding USDT0. That is what the flag still guards.

- `usdt0_bridge_enabled`: needs one small transfer **per direction**, including `ethereum→arbitrum` — the only leg with an approve step.
- `cctp_generic_rail_enabled`: **must not** be flipped without `cctp_generic_relayer_enabled`, and the relayer wallet needs native gas

author: sdelcore
body:
## What this is

**Primarily a `nixpkgs-unstable` bump.** Adding the `hunk` CLI is the motivation, but the bulk of the diff is repairing the localllm/vllm stack afterwards. Please review it as a toolchain bump, not as "add a CLI tool".

`nixpkgs-unstable` moves `d407951` → `0954f7e` (2026-07-05 → 2026-07-29). No other flake input was touched.

The bump moves the default Python interpreter **3.13 → 3.14**, which is what caused all of the fallout below.

## localllm fixes caused by the bump

All in `nix/modules/software/localllm/vllm.nix`.

### 1. `permittedInsecurePackages` rename

The allow entry was `python3.13-vllm-0.16.0`. That name embeds the interpreter, so it is now `python3.14-vllm-0.16.0`. vllm itself is **unchanged at 0.16.0**.

Worth a look: the old comment described 3 CVEs. nixpkgs now catalogues **15** against this same version. The installed artifact is no different than before — nixpkgs just knows more about it — but the comment was updated to stop implying the list is short. The headline issue is still CVE-2026-27893 (RCE via `trust_remote_code` when loading untrusted models), which does not apply to how this module is used (local on-demand CLI, self-chosen models, no exposed API server).

### 2. `tensorflow-bin: unsupported configuration: x86_64-linux_314`

Traced with `--show-trace` before fixing. The chain is:

```
system-path → vllm → outlines (nativeBuildInputs) → tensorflow
```

`outlines` is a **runtime** dep of vllm, so it can't be dropped. It gates its test phase on `doCheck = !config.cudaSupport`. This module's `import inputs.nixpkgs-unstable` leaves `cudaSupport` at its default, so outlines' tests are enabled, which drags in its whole `nativeCheckInputs` list — including `tensorflow`. `tensorflow` is `tensorflow-bin`, which only ships prebuilt wheels for interpreters upstream publishes, and there is no 3.14 wheel.

Fix: disable outlines' check phase. Setting `cudaSupport = true` would also make the error go away (it flips `doCheck` to false), but that would silently rebuild vllm as a CUDA package — a much larger, user-visible change. Took the narrow route.

### 3. `model-hosting-container-standards` test failures (not anticipated)

A third regression surfaced after the tensorflow fix. This is AWS's SageMaker hosting shim, also a **runtime** dep of vllm. Version is **unchanged at 0.1.14** across the bump — only the interpreter moved — and 10 of its tests now fail.

Confirmed upstream, not caused by anything here: building `python3Packages.model-hosting-container-standards` from plain `github:nixos/nixpkgs/0954f7e` produces the **identical derivation hash** and the identical 10 failures.

The failures are real, not flaky — decorator/env-var handler registration no longer takes effect, so SageMaker's `/ping` and `/invocations` override machinery is broken under 3.14. That machinery only matters when vllm runs inside a SageMaker container; this module runs it as a local CLI. Skipped those 10 by name and kept the other ~700 running, rather than disabling the whole check phase.

## Patch re-verification

- **`L2_cache_size()` source patch — KEPT.** `torch` is 2.12.0 in *both* the old and new pin, and vllm is still 0.16.0, so the missing `at::cpu::L2_cache_size()` symbol is unchanged. Patch still applies and is still needed.
- **starlette constraint patch — DROPPED, fixed upstream.** `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` went 7.1.0 → 8.0.2. 7.1.0 declared `starlette (>=0.30.0,<1.0.0)` while nixpkgs shipped starlette 1.x, hence the override. 8.0.2 now declares `starlette (>=1.0.0,<2.0.0)`, which the pinned starlette 1.3.1 satisfies. Verified by reading `pyproject.toml` in the 8.0.2 source. Removed outright rather than loosened.

## The actual feature

`hunk` 0.17.3 added to `home.packages` in `home/modules/claude-code/default.nix` — a terminal diff viewer for reviewing agent-written changesets.

It uses a direct `import inputs.nixpkgs-unstable` (the pattern already used across `nix/modules/software/localllm/`) rather than `pkgs.unstable.hunk`. The `unstable` overlay is applied at `nixpkgs.overlays` in `mkSystem`, and `home-manager.useGlobalPkgs` is never set, so Home Manager's `pkgs` does not carry that overlay.

## Heads-up: likely merge conflict

The open `trim-skills-and-claude-md` branch also edits `home/modules/claude-code/default.nix`, removing an obsidian plugin block from `home.file`. This PR edits `home.packages` and the `let` block in the same file. Different hunks, but expect git to need a hand depending on merge order.

## Verification

- `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.nightman.config.system.build.toplevel` — passes (full vllm + llama.cpp CUDA rebuild)
- `nix build .#nixosConfigurations.dayman.config.system.build.toplevel` — passes
- `hunk-0.17.3` confirmed present in both closures; `tensorflow` absent from both

No `just switch` / `just deploy` was run — build verification only.

## One thing I did not change

While tracing the tensorflow issue I noticed this module's nixpkgs instance leaves `cudaSupport` at its default (unlike `llama-swap.nix`, which sets `cudaSupport = true`), so **vllm here appears to be a CPU build**. That contradicts the existing comment on the `L2_cache_size` patch, which says "we run on CUDA". This is pre-existing and unrelated to the bump, and changing it would be a significant user-visible change to the localllm setup, so I left it alone. Flagging it as possibly worth a separate look.

author: jirawatpyk
body:
## Incident

Prod intermittently **CSP-blocks ALL JavaScript** on authenticated, Suspense-heavy `/admin/**` pages (renewals, tasks, members, invoices). Console: Next chunk scripts + the inline bootstrap "violates `script-src 'self' 'nonce-…' 'strict-dynamic' 'unsafe-inline' https://js.stripe.com`". Because `'strict-dynamic'` disables `'self'`, any script whose nonce ≠ the header nonce is blocked; the blocked inline bootstrap breaks the trust chain and every chunk cascades → the SPA router never hydrates (every navigation degrades to a full `document` load). "Refresh sometimes fixes it." Sign-in pages are always fine.

## Root cause (5-agent RCA + on-the-wire capture)

- The authed document is **fresh** — `x-vercel-cache: MISS`, `age: 0`, `cache-control: private, no-store`; the response CSP-header nonce **==** the `Link:` preload nonces. So it is **NOT caching**, **NOT a stale deployment**, **NOT a CDN**, **NOT the domain** (`zyncdata.app` is the deprecated alias, but both it and `dxtspace.com` serve the same current deployment with identical healthy sign-in nonces), and **NOT PR #299** (that change is additive, plain `<a>`, no prefetch; the page was already dynamic).
- The real cause: `proxy()` minted a per-request nonce, wrote it into the **response** CSP header, and forwarded only **`x-nonce`** on the request. Next.js derives the nonce it stamps onto its bootstrap **and streamed (Suspense-boundary) scripts** from the **request's `Content-Security-Policy` header** (the canonical Next nonce-middleware pattern). With only `x-nonce` forwarded, streamed / dynamically-loaded (Turbopack) chunk scripts were intermittently un-nonced on Suspense-heavy pages → blocked under `'strict-dynamic'`. Sign-in streams nothing, so all its scripts were in the initial nonced batch → always worked.
- Known Next.js issue class: vercel/next.js #89754, discussion #81703, #55638 — nonce enforcement is fragile with Next 16 streaming / Turbopack.

## Fix

In the pass-through path, `proxy()` now ALSO sets `Content-Security-Policy: buildCsp(env.isDevelopment, nonce)` on the **forwarded request** headers (same `nonce` as the response CSP), matching the canonical Next.js pattern. So request-CSP nonce ≡ response-CSP nonce ≡ every stamped-script nonce.

- **CSP itself is UNCHANGED** — `buildCsp` untouched; prod stays `'self' 'nonce-X' 'strict-dynamic' 'unsafe-inline' https://js.stripe.com`. **No security weakening.** This is the strong-CSP-preserving fix (option A); webpack build (B) / dropping the nonce (C) were the fallbacks if this did not hold.
- Additive; the existing `x-nonce` forward is kept.

## Tests / gates

- `pnpm typecheck` clean · `pnpm lint` (proxy.ts + test) clean
- `tests/unit/proxy/` **21/21** — new `forwarded-csp-nonce.test.ts` asserts the forwarded **request** CSP nonce === the response CSP nonce (and the `x-nonce` forward matches), via the `x-middleware-request-content-security-policy` encoding.

## Verification (before merge to prod)

The bug only reproduces on **authenticated** Suspense-heavy pages, which a preview deploy's isolated per-PR DB can't easily exercise (no admin account). Options: (a) seed an admin on the preview DB branch and test `/admin/renewals/tasks` on the preview URL; (b) given the change is additive + canonical + cannot weaken/worsen CSP, merge to prod after CI + security review and verify on prod with redeploy rollback ready. Security-engineer review requested.

author: adamstddrd
body:
Closes #60.

## What changed

- the auth-failure classifier now catches opencode's verbatim status-text passthrough -- the issue's exact `Error: Unauthorized: Unauthorized` matched nothing in the old pattern (no "401", no "api key" phrasing), so it reported as a bare crash with no hint at all
- the hint now names everything the framework knows: the resolved provider, the `baseURL` when `opencode.json` declares one, and the credential the run injected -- or that none was stored:

  ```
  provider authentication failed -- my_gateway at https://gateway.example.com/v1/compat rejected the run's my_gateway_api_key credential (openroutines credentials set my_gateway_api_key)
  ```

- new `ProviderBaseURL` accessor on the framework's `opencode.json` view; its comment addresses the config boundary head-on -- quoting an endpoint in a diagnostic is not interpreting it, and the framework still never requests against it
- docs: the "curl the `baseURL` directly" debugging recipe in getting-started's provider section, grounded in why the config boundary makes that test faithful

## Secrets

No credential value can reach the hint, by construction: `authHint` receives the model string, a directory, and a boolean -- no secret material enters the function. The injected-or-not check reads key presence only. The tail the classifier matches on is already scrubbed against the run's credential values before capture.

## Deliberately not included

The issue's second half -- a `check`-time probe of the provider endpoint -- is a real design decision, not a patch: `check` is the documented non-acting validation path and is made for CI, where a live network probe adds flakiness and requires the master key. Left open in the issue; a design entry (or a separate `credentials verify` command) can pick it up.

author: monosans
body:
## What's wrong

The SOCKS4 connector writes one byte too many in its CONNECT request.

A SOCKS4 request is an 8-byte header followed by a **user ID** — a variable-length string ended by a single zero byte:

```
VN(1) CD(1) DSTPORT(2) DSTIP(4) USERID(variable) NULL(1)
```

— [_SOCKS: A protocol for TCP proxy across firewalls_](https://www.openssh.com/txt/socks4.protocol), Ying-Da Lee

This connector never sends a user ID, so that field is empty and only its single terminating zero byte belongs on the wire — 9 bytes in total. `Request::write_to_buf` in `src/client/legacy/connect/proxy/socks/v4/messages.rs` wrote _two_ zero bytes (one commented `USERID`, one commented `NULL`), so it sent 10.

## Why it matters

The SOCKS4a extension — the one that lets the _proxy_ resolve a domain name — puts the hostname immediately after that terminator, itself ended by a zero byte:

```
VN(1) CD(1) DSTPORT(2) DSTIP(4) USERID(variable) NULL(1) HOSTNAME(variable) NULL(1)
```

— [_SOCKS 4A: A Simple Extension to SOCKS 4 Protocol_](https://www.openssh.com/txt/socks4a.protocol), Ying-Da Lee

That is this connector's default mode: `local_dns` is off by default, so a domain destination is sent by name for the proxy to resolve. With an extra zero byte in front of it, the proxy reads the hostname field as an empty string, and the real hostname is never part of the request at all.

Feeding both versions of the bytes to a parser that follows the spec literally:

```
SOCKS4a BEFORE (19 bytes): port=443 ip=0.0.0.255 userid="" hostname=""         leftover="hyper.rs\0"
SOCKS4a AFTER  (18 bytes): port=443 ip=0.0.0.255 userid="" hostname="hyper.rs" leftover=""
SOCKS4  BEFORE (10 bytes): port=443 ip=127.0.0.1 userid="" (no hostname)       leftover="\0"
SOCKS4  AFTER  ( 9 bytes): port=443 ip=127.0.0.1 userid="" (no hostname)       leftover=""
```

In other words:

- **SOCKS4a (domain destination — the default) is broken.** The proxy gets an empty hostname and the request fails. Worse, the leftover `hyper.rs\0` stays in the proxy's receive buffer and is relayed into the tunnel as if the client had sent it as application data.
- **Plain SOCKS4 (IPv4 destination) still connects**, because the address travels in DSTIP — but the leftover zero byte is still there and reaches the target as a stray first byte of the tunneled stream.

As an independent check, curl builds the same request with exactly one terminator: in `lib/socks.c` it appends `strlen(user) + 1` bytes for the user ID (just the terminator when there is no user), then `strlen(hostname) + 1` for SOCKS4a.

## The change

- Remove the extra zero byte, and adjust the two `remaining_mut()` checks and the returned lengths from `10` to `9`.
- Add `test_socks_v4a_with_server_resolved_domain_works`. The domain path had no test at all, which is how this went unnoticed since the connectors landed in #187 — the existing `test_socks_v4_works` only covers the IPv4 path, where the bug is much less visible.
- Fix one comment on the line being touched: `buf.put_u16(*port)` was labelled `// IP`.

No public API change; the only behavioural difference is one fewer byte on the wire. `cargo test --all-features --test proxy` passes.

- `bin/check-playbook.sh`: every entry now requires **`Scope`** (closed enum `loop|maintainer`, fail-closed on missing/unknown) and validates **`Bound-in`** (mandatory value on `maintainer`, forbidden presence on `loop`; shape-only — non-empty, no absolute path, no `~`, never touches the filesystem). The other three directions stay legal: issue #23's one-ledger rationale explicitly requires a local lesson that generalises to name its universal replacement (maintainer→loop).

- `bin/playbook-promote.sh`: required `--scope` (no default — a default would silently classify), pass-through `--bound-in`. Combination rules are deliberately NOT re-implemented — the checker's re-validation is the single authority. Codex round 1 caught an explicitly-blank `--bound-in` being silently dropped before re-validation; fixed with a parse-time `BOUND_IN_SEEN` flag so the checker judges every CLI-supplied signal.

author: bukka
body:
Receiving a stream is quadratic in the number of frames the peer sends. Inserting a frame that is not a simple append at the tail scans the frame list from the head, and the list is bounded only by the stream flow control window, with gaps counting towards it. Sending one byte frames at even offsets and then filling the odd ones takes 35 seconds of CPU for 262144 frames, which is about half of what the default 512 KiB window permits. Frames are also never merged, so even a gapless stream keeps one list entry per frame received until the application reads it, and each entry pins the packet it arrived in.

Looking at how other implementations avoid this, both nginx and ngtcp2 copy received stream data into fixed size chunks (4 KiB and 8 KiB respectively) rather than keeping references to the packets. That is what decouples their bookkeeping from the number of frames received and ties it to the bytes actually buffered instead. It turned out we already have most of the machinery for this: `ossl_sframe_list_move_data()` copies the data out and merges frames that have become contiguous, but it has never been called, because the ring buffer it writes into is always created with size 0. So this replaces that ring buffer with a list of chunks allocated on demand and calls the copy once a stream accumulates enough frames. A stream received in order then collapses to a single list entry however many frames it arrived in, and the packets are released.

Copying alone is not enough, because frames separated by gaps still cannot be merged, and with the copy pass in place the quadratic simply moves from the insert scan into the copy walk. So there is still a limit on how many entries the list may hold, set to 4000 to match ngtcp2, which rejects the same condition once its reorder buffer holds 4000 gaps and raised that from 1000 to cope with high loss and large flow control windows.

This overlaps with #32126, which limits the number of buffered frames without changing anything else. That one is deliberately minimal and derives its limit from the flow control window, because without merging the limit has to tolerate  a peer sending many small frames in order. Here the merging does that work, so the limit can be a plain constant and only ever triggers on genuinely fragmented streams. If this is acceptable then #32126 is not needed, otherwise #32126 stands on its own as the smaller change.

author: brueshi
body:
Blocks get a per-block chrome layer: a grip and a `+` beside the hovered block, drag-to-reorder, and a gutter sweep that selects a contiguous run for delete, marks and Turn into.

Fixes SKR-124

## What changed

**Model ops.** `moveBlock` and `insertBlockBefore` join `removeBlocks` and the table move ops in `range-ops`. `moveBlock` takes an insertion boundary rather than a final index, so it maps straight from a drop indicator, and returns null on the boundaries flanking the block so a no-op drag earns no undo step. Both are top-level only: lifting a nested block out of its container would be an outdent wearing a reorder's clothes, and `list-ops` already owns outdenting.

**Seam handling.** A `gapBefore` holds the verbatim bytes before a block and the serializer honours it wherever the block ends up. A naive reorder is therefore silently corrupting: a block carrying a blank-line seam dropped at the top opens the file on a blank line, and the block promoted to first glues itself to nothing. Both ops clear the seams a move disturbs and hand them back to the reconstruction rule. `dirty` is left alone, so a clean block still emits its source byte-pristine.

**Chrome.** `block-chrome` follows `table-chrome`'s architecture one level up: the layer sits in the scroller but outside the contenteditable, slots are placed in content coordinates so they ride scroll with no listener, and it rebuilds off the structural-change signal rather than the keystroke path. The visual language is the table handles', since a block grip and a table row grip sit inches apart in one document. Both slots centre on the block's first line, so a long paragraph carries its grip where the writer is reading. The cluster straddles the surface's left padding and shifts right to stay on canvas in a window narrower than the measure.

**Reorder.** The drop commits "before which block", not an index. `orderForDisplay` gathers footnote definitions into a document-end footer, so an index taken from the screen would address a different block in the model whenever a definition sat above the drop. Definitions are excluded from the reorder outright, since the footer is a generated view rather than a place to arrange things.

**Sweep.** A new gesture, not a new selection model: the block-selection state was already plural and its delete already folded extra ids into one `removeBlocks` call, so a swept range is one undo step by construction. Marks and Turn into needed a single seam — both already map over `selectedLeaves`, but a block selection clears the DOM selection, so `selectedLeaves` now resolves its leaves from the model. Barriers yield no leaves, so a range holding a divider or table marks its prose and skips the rest instead of refusing.

## Why these choices

The sweep starts in the gutter only. A drag beginning in the text is already text selection, and a modifier-held band over the prose would be undiscoverable as well as ambiguous against the reorder drag. Below the move threshold the press stays what it was, so a plain margin click still places a caret.

Every activation binds to `click`, not `pointerup`, because WKWebView drops `pointerup` on a motionless press. Drags use pointer events on the scroller and window rather than capturing the tiny grip, and tear down on `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, or the click that closes a motionless press.

The caret deliberately stays put across a reorder rather than following the moved block: the writer is pointing, not typing.

## What to verify

- Hover a block: grip and `+` appear beside its first line. `+` inserts an empty paragraph above and lands the caret in it.
- Drag a grip: the block dims, a drop line tracks the nearest seam, release commits. One undo reverses it.
- Press a grip without moving: selects, does not start a drag.
- Sweep down the gutter across several blocks, then Backspace: the whole range goes in one undo step. Then try Cmd-B and Turn into over a swept range.
- A plain click in the margin still places a caret, unchanged.
- Drag across a document with footnotes: the definition footer is not a drop target and blocks land where the indicator said.

## Gates

Typecheck clean, 129 files / 1503 tests, latency matrix 64/64. Verified in the macOS shell, not only in Chromium.

### Motivation

- Introduce an ASP.NET Core migration foundation so the platform can be migrated route-by-route while keeping the existing PHP runtime authoritative during parity work. 
- Provide explicit diagnostics, parity reporters, and a route-cutover policy to make cutover decisions observable and testable without switching production traffic. 
- Add worker scaffolding and deployment guardrails so PHP cron jobs and operator workflows can be migrated safely with dry-run and rollback controls.

### Description

- Add a new `aspnet/` solution containing `EcomAE.Platform` (Web) and `EcomAE.Workers` (Worker) projects with routing, modules (CP/ERP/BOS/Storefront/API), middleware (`TenantResolutionMiddleware`, `RouteCutoverDecisionMiddleware`), and many migration/parity reporter types. 
- Implement tenant/route resolution, legacy session bridge, legacy API key parsing and policy contracts, price lookup abstractions and repository scaffolding, migration parity/readiness/progress/cutover reporters, and a surface shell catalog for placeholder UI payloads. 
- Add worker job catalog, planner, runner and placeholder background service plus supporting DTOs and schedule plans, and wire authorization constants/policies and module registration in `Program.cs`. 
- Add deployment/runbook artifacts and safety tooling including systemd unit templates, nginx diagnostic includes, `preflight` and `deploy` scripts, proxy guardrail verifier, consolidation/rebase helper scripts, live-smoke tooling, PHP alias router `content/general_pages/epc_portal_route_aliases.php`, minor PHP fixes (index and templates) and an `.htaccess` tweak to make /bos rewrites case-insensitive.

### Testing

- Unit tests were added under `aspnet/tests/EcomAE.Platform.Tests` and executed with `dotnet test aspnet/tests/EcomAE.Platform.Tests`. 
- A detailed foundation verification script `tests/aspnet_migration/run_detailed_foundation_tests.sh` was provided that runs PHP lint (`php -l`), shell syntax checks (`bash -n`), proxy-guardrail checks (`scripts/verify_aspnet_proxy_guardrails.sh`) and optional live smoke; this script was exercised as part of the preflight/deploy flow. 
- Deployment preflight `scripts/preflight_aspnet_production.sh` and guardrail verification `scripts/verify_aspnet_proxy_guardrails.sh` are included and were used to validate environment, file permissions, and config snippets. 
- All added automated unit and foundation checks were run as part of the local verification flow and reported green in the foundation verification run.

## What

Hope & Fear's **12 martial stance texts** had nowhere to live. Adds `MartialStance` as a standalone entity with full CRUD + `/bulk`.

Migration `V20260730130448355__create_martial_stances_table.sql` — `martial_stances` (name, description, tier with a 1-4 CHECK, expansion FK, `is_official`, `created_by_user_id`, `original_martial_stance_id` self-FK, soft delete) plus a `martial_stance_features` join table. Closer structural match than `Weapon`: name / tier / expansion / `isOfficial` / `createdBy` / features / `deletedAt` via `BaseItem`, its own `description` TEXT, and an `originalX` self-FK for custom copies. Weapon's trait/range/burden/damage fields don't apply to a stance.

Verified — not assumed — that **Loot's create *and* bulk-create both call `.isOfficial(request.getIsOfficial())`**, so the hardcoded-`false` bulk bug CORE-01 found in Adversary doesn't exist in this lineage and was safe to copy. `pdf-structure.md`'s own note ("new data model needed: `martial_stance` entity with `tier`, `name`, `text`") independently confirms the shape.

## Search registration

`SearchableEntityType.MARTIAL_STANCE`, `@SearchIndexed`, `buildForMartialStance()` (Weight A name, Weight B description, Weight C feature text — same shape as `buildForLoot`), plus arms in `SearchIndexService.resolveRepository()` and `SearchService.resolveEntity()`.

Rebased onto #55, keeping main's real Beastform arms (`beastformRepository`, `beastformService.getBeastformById`) with `MARTIAL_STANCE` alongside. Verified by grep: no `null` return survives in either switch.

## Verification

`./mvnw verify` — **708 tests, 0 failures** (up from a 684 baseline; `MartialStanceServiceTest` + `MartialStanceControllerIntegrationTest` add ~24).

Against real Postgres on a fresh volume: 71 migrations applied, `grep -c FlywayException` → **0**.

- Full CRUD — create → 201, get → 200, update → 200, delete → 204 then 404, restore → 200 with `deletedAt` cleared.
- `/bulk` with **all 12 real Hope & Fear stance texts** in one POST (Favored/Invigorating/Quick/Reliable T1, Aggressive/Anchored/Evasive/Vigilant T2, Relentless/Precise T3, Unshakable/Deadly T4) → 201, array of 12; row count confirmed at 13 including an earlier single-create.

author: aswinsam
body:
M3, first half. Work that used to happen only in a foreground terminal can now be queued, run in its own process, watched, and cancelled. The HTTP layer follows in a separate change; this is the part where the hard correctness lives.

Each job runs the ordinary command line in a child process, rather than a second execution path. That is not incidental: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES is read when torch is imported and cannot be changed afterwards, so per-job GPU selection is only possible by setting it before the interpreter starts. Reusing the CLI also means a queued job behaves exactly like the command a user would type, which is what makes its failures reproducible.

Scheduling has two rules. At most one accelerator job runs at a time, because VRAM cannot be partitioned on consumer hardware — two runs sharing a card do not get half each, they contend and the second dies. Everything else may overlap, so preparing a corpus does not wait behind a twelve-hour training run.

- SQLite with WAL, no ORM: the point of dropping Docker was to need no services, and an ORM is a dependency every install carries for one table
- process identity is PID plus creation time, so a supervisor restarting after a reboot cannot adopt whatever now holds that number
- a job the server was running when it died becomes INTERRUPTED, which is distinct from FAILED: the work did not fail, we simply stopped watching
- cancellation kills the process tree children-first, terminate before kill, so a trainer can finish the checkpoint it is midway through
- memory caps use cgroups via systemd-run where available. RLIMIT_AS was rejected: it caps virtual address space, and CUDA reserves enormous amounts it never touches, so the cap would kill healthy processes. Where no cap can be applied the job records that, rather than implying a limit is in force
- only parameters named in a fixed table reach the command line, so a request cannot introduce an argument the CLI does not already accept

Three bugs found by exercising it rather than reading it. Cancel looked up a pid on the wrong object and had never been run. Schema creation committed implicitly inside a transaction the helper then tried to commit again. And the queue ordered by a timestamp with second resolution, so any burst of submissions tied and fell back to the random job id — FIFO was broken for the ordinary case of submitting several jobs at once. It now orders by insertion, which also survives an NTP step backwards.

478 tests, ruff and mypy clean.

author: simeon-code254
body:
## Summary

AfyaConnect — an accessibility-first telemedicine app for people with disabilities in Kenya (quadriplegia, paraplegia, ALS, MS, and related mobility impairments). This PR adds the full Expo/React Native mobile app plus a working backend integration.

**Mobile app (12 screens, all four accessibility paths on every screen):**
- Spoken (TTS announces each screen on arrival, in the user's language)
- Single-input auto-scan (for switch / sip-and-puff users; disables itself when a screen reader is active so it doesn't fight VoiceOver/TalkBack)
- Full screen-reader semantics (roles, labels, states, hints, live regions)
- Large touch targets, scaled per accessibility profile
- Bilingual throughout (English + Kiswahili), with every clinical/medical Kiswahili term flagged in `mobile/src/i18n/NEEDS_SW_REVIEW.md` for a fluent clinical reviewer before real use

**Backend:** adopted a teammate's more complete async FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + Postgres backend (JWT access/refresh tokens, timing-safe login, bilingual triage with language auto-detect, audit logging, Alembic migrations) as canonical, and added the pieces the mobile app still needed (`GET /appointments`, a scoped `POST /audit/log`, CORS allowlist).

**Verified for real**, not just written: provisioned an actual Postgres database, ran the Alembic migration, exercised the backend with 39 automated checks against the live DB, then drove the mobile app through registration → accessibility setup → real symptom triage → real appointment booking, confirming the resulting rows directly in the database, with zero console errors.

That testing caught and fixed four real bugs:
- **Patient-safety bug:** the triage engine silently mis-triaged critical English symptoms as "low" priority for any patient whose saved language preference was Kiswahili, when the request didn't explicitly say what language the symptom text was in (every symptom preset always sends English clinical text). Mobile now always sends an explicit `language` on every triage report.
- Assistive-tech values (`switch`, `sip_puff`, `voice`) were silently collapsing to `"none"` for exactly the three accessibility profiles this app exists to serve, due to a DB-enum vs. API-enum value mismatch.
- Postgres enum inserts were failing entirely for every disability/assistive-tech/priority/status column.
- `/auth/me` and the triage response were missing fields the mobile app needs (profile medical/caregiver/address data; the triage record's own ID, without which no appointment could ever be booked).

`USE_MOCK` defaults to `true` in `mobile/src/services/api.js`, so the app runs standalone with no backend required; flip it to `false` once a backend is deployed and reachable.

## Test plan

- [x] 39/39 backend checks passing against a live Postgres database (auth, profile, triage EN/SW, appointments, audit, queue, CORS)
- [x] Full mobile app run against the real backend: register → accessibility setup → symptom report → triage → appointment booking, verified against real DB rows, zero console errors
- [x] Full mobile app run in mock/standalone mode (no backend), same flow, zero console errors
- [x] All 12 screens screenshotted and manually reviewed across touch, voice, switch, sip-and-puff, eye-tracking, and head-mouse profiles
- [ ] Manual VoiceOver (iOS) / TalkBack (Android) pass on a real device — not done in this environment, flagged as the one remaining checklist item
- [ ] Kiswahili clinical terms reviewed by a fluent speaker with medical background — flagged in `NEEDS_SW_REVIEW.md`, not yet done

author: filipisantoss93
vaggeliska
body:
`Int(someDouble)` **terminates the process** for NaN, an infinity, or anything past
`Int64` — it traps, it does not throw. Four separate agents hit this class during the
extraction waves and fixed it locally at the site they were touching. This is the sweep.

## Triage

105 `Int(` matches. Not all convert a float:

| | count | |
|---|---|---|
| Reachable float conversions, converted | **88** | across 40 files |
| Not floating-point | 3 | `Int(String)` returns nil, never traps |
| Comment/doc mentions | ~10 | untouched |
| Already guarded, left alone | 3 | see below |

Reachable means the value arrives from user input, HealthKit or the food API: calorie
sums, portion grams, serving counts, heights, TDEE/BMR, macro ratios, API pack quantities,
active energy.

`ActivityCalorieBudget.roundedConsumed` was the worst of them — it sums raw logged-entry
calories with no guard, and `remaining`, `overAmount` and `isOver` all hang off it.

## Three sites deliberately left converting

- `Double.truncatedSafely` itself.
- `NutritionCalculator.defaultTarget` — its `max(1200, …)` floors NaN and it range-checks
  first. Its `.max`-for-infinity is deliberate and correct for a calorie *target*, where
  `truncatedSafely`'s 0 would be actively wrong.
- `HistoryChartIndexAxis.slot(for:)` — already guards `isFinite` and the domain.

## Two findings that were not straight substitution

**`truncatedSafely` was the wrong answer once.** `HistoryCalorieTrendProjection.point(for:)`
is a lookup, not a readout — returning 0 for NaN would silently select day one for a garbage
gesture value rather than rejecting it. Its sibling `HistoryChartIndexAxis.slot(for:)` already
guarded; this now matches it. Separate commit (9c75db6).

**`PortionSelection.normalizedGramStep` had a second overflow behind the first.** It multiplied
the converted quotient by the step size *in `Int`*, so a value clamped to `.max` would then
trap on the multiply. The multiply moved into `Double`, ahead of the conversion.

## One duplication accepted

`CalorynShared/WidgetSnapshot.swift` cannot use `truncatedSafely` — `Caloryn/Extensions/` is
app-target only, and moving it to `CalorynShared` would put a duplicate `Double` extension in
the test target alongside `@testable import Caloryn`, making the member ambiguous. The guard is
spelled out inline with a comment saying why. Flagged rather than hidden.

## Lint

New `trapping_int_conversion` custom rule at **error** severity; `swiftlint lint` is clean, so
no downgrade was needed. It was proved able to fail by reintroducing a conversion.

It bans the `Int(x.rounded())` form only. A bare `Int(_:)` is indistinguishable by regex from
the safe `Int(someInt)` / `Int(someString)`, so the rule catches the shape the crash actually
arrived in rather than attempting the whole class and forcing suppressions everywhere.

## Tests

`CalorynTests/NonFiniteNumberSafetyTests.swift` — 15 cases feeding NaN / ±infinity / `1e30`
through public entry points and asserting **the result**, not merely the absence of a crash.

- 548 → **563** XCTest (+15)
- 579 swift-testing, **unchanged** — which is this PR's warrant: no valid-input behaviour moved.

`Caloryn-All` passes: 563 + 579 unit, 17 UI journeys, no retries.

author: anunay999
body:
## What & why

Recall previously discarded query-to-node cosine distance after hybrid search and ranked candidates from ordinal match rank, activation, and degree only. This adds the designed semantic-alignment term, carries hop-0 distance into recall candidates, and neutrally imputes unknown distances from the mean known alignment. Lexical-only hits and graph neighbors are neither rewarded nor sunk; when every distance is unknown, the semantic term is a constant. The composite uses the exact envelope-preserving weights from Backlog #10 and leaves the existing tie-break chain unchanged.

The ACT-R noise term remains deliberately unshipped so ranking stays deterministic.

## How it was tested

- `npm run typecheck`
- focused retrieval-fixes suite in memory mode: 19 passed, 0 failed, 1 expected skip
- focused retrieval-fixes suite against PostgreSQL: 20 passed, 0 failed
- full memory suite: 131 passed, 0 failed, 1 expected skip
- full PostgreSQL suite: 152 passed, 0 failed
- mutation T1: setting `0.30 * align` to zero fails F10a on both drivers (`aligned index 2` vs `weaker index 1`)
- mutation T2: mapping unknown distance to zero fails F10b on both drivers (`lexical-only index 2`, last)

## Checklist

- [x] `npm run typecheck` passes
- [x] Relevant `*:test` suites pass locally against memory and PostgreSQL
- [x] No secrets, tokens, or real connection strings in the diff
- [x] Docs updated for the activation-ranking behavior
